titre: Gulf Air's Continuous Improvement Journey with Microsoft Foundry
contenu: On November 9, Gulf Air reached a milestone: two AI agents in its Falcon Eye application—a voice agent and a chat agent—went live for users. The milestone did not come from finding one perfect prompt. Gulf Air had spent weeks building a demanding pool of evaluation questions, studying traces, finding gaps, changing instructions and code, and testing again. Ahmed reported that the team generated approximately 10,000 candidate questions across different business perspectives, then ran selected questions in smaller batches to exercise real aviation and management logic. Ahmed AbdulJalil Ebrahim described the impact plainly: " What evaluation, insights, and optimize did for us was really amazing. We were able to fix business logic the agent had not understood." For us, the important part of this story is not that one tool produced one answer. It is that Gulf Air assembled a repeatable improvement practice around the hard questions its business would actually ask. The application had to do more than retrieve an answer Falcon Eye is an important Gulf Air application used for operational analysis and management decision support. Ahmed described a five-agent vision spanning UI summaries, smart search, dynamic reporting, real-time voice, and a reasoning chat experience. These agents connect to operational data through APIs and a Postgres MCP. They can analyze information, perform calculations, and help users create reports or dashboards. That makes them useful, but it also raises the quality bar. A simple factual test cannot establish whether an agent: selected the right operational field for the user's question; followed an aviation-specific rule; generated an appropriate query; performed a calculation correctly; preserved the user's data permissions; or remained reliable when the same intent appeared in a different form. For senior leaders asking operational or financial questions, a fluent answer is not enough. The reasoning path and the business result both matter. Gulf Air built an evaluation pool around the hardest business questions Ahmed described this generated question pool as covering multiple business perspectives. He emphasized that these were not only straightforward questions such as total departures or delays. They were intended to test the business logic that had been difficult to express through a system prompt alone. The team selected questions from that pool and generally ran them in batches of 100. The evaluation results separated successful answers, failures, no-answers, and errors. Gulf Air then examined the resulting traces and insights, brought the evidence into VS Code with its engineering context, implemented changes, and evaluated again. The loop looked like this: Run difficult evaluation questions -> inspect failures, no-answers, and errors -> review generated insights and supporting traces -> bring the evidence into the coding workflow -> change instructions, tools, or application logic -> test candidate improvements -> add independent human review -> run evaluation again Human review was a deliberate part of the process. Other team members approached the agent differently and documented issues that the original test design had missed. Their findings became new inputs to the next improvement cycle. Immediately before our November 9 conversation, Ahmed had completed another 400-question run and applied additional fixes. This was not a one-time benchmark. It was an operating rhythm. Evidence became useful when it entered the engineering workflow The workflow did not stop at an evaluation score or a list of traces. Gulf Air used the evidence to decide what to change. Insights from traces helped group recurring behaviors and connect them with representative executions. VS Code supplied the surrounding engineering context: code, APIs, MCP access, reports, and prior findings. The team could then investigate whether an issue came from instructions, tool behavior, application logic, or the test itself. This distinction matters. An insight can identify a pattern and point to a likely direction, but it is not automatically a validated fix. Gulf Air still reviewed the evidence, implemented the change in the appropriate system, and ran the agent again. That developer-led pattern is also central to the latest Microsoft Foundry experience: Scheduled and on-demand analysis can process new traces incrementally after the initial lookback. Linked and highlighted traces let developers inspect the evidence behind an insight. Custom categories and additional instructions help focus future analysis on business-specific concerns. A proposed change can be copied into a coding workflow when the issue belongs in code or application configuration. For eligible instruction or tool-description issues, developers can use fix insights and create an agent optimizer run. The handoff is important, but so is its boundary: a proposed fix is a starting point for validation, not an automatic production change. From a selected insight to an evaluated candidate From the Insights tab, a developer can choose Select insights , select the relevant insights, and choose Fix insights to create an optimization run. Foundry uses the selected evidence to prepare supported replay scenarios, proposes candidate changes, and compares them with the current agent version as the baseline. The goal is not to accept whichever candidate has the highest single score. Developers can inspect: which selected issues improved; the candidate's actual instruction or tool-description changes; per-scenario and overall evaluation results; quality comparisons with the baseline; token usage and estimated cost; latency; and whether independent conversations were available to check for broader regressions. Sometimes the responsible result is still the baseline. A candidate might fix one failure while regressing elsewhere, the evaluator might find the result inconclusive, or the available evidence might be too narrow. The developer reviews those trade-offs and explicitly decides whether to promote a candidate. Nothing in this workflow automatically changes the active agent. Human review, promotion, testing, and production activation remain separate decisions. Gulf Air assembled this handoff manually. The new select-insights-to-fix experience is designed to shorten part of that journey by carrying verified insight evidence into a controlled optimization run. Confidence was the business outcome The value of this work was not a single score or a one-time test. Each evaluation cycle produced reusable evidence - failure cases, traces, human-reviewed findings, and proposed changes that the team could carry into the next iteration. Validation became part of the engineering workflow rather than a final checkpoint before launch. The business outcome was confidence. Ahmed described the workflow as giving Gulf Air a level of confidence in its agents that the team had not achieved before. He also reported that Gulf Air management was impressed by the voice and chat-agent demonstration on launch day. From Gulf Air: what changed for our team “The agent refinement experience changed the way we approach agent AI development at Gulf Air. Instead of relying on individual tests or continually adjusting prompts, we can systematically challenge our agents with thousands of real business questions, understand where they struggle, and use evaluation, traces and insights to identify the underlying issues. This approach helps us refine how agents understand complex aviation business logic and gives our teams greater confidence in the agents we move into production. More importantly, it establishes a continuous development cycle where real-world usage and evaluation drive the next improvement. ” Five lessons for teams moving agents into production Gulf Air's experience suggests five practical lessons. 1. Build the evaluation set around business difficulty Start with the questions your business struggles to encode, not only the questions your agent already answers well. Include ambiguity, calculations, tool use, permissions, and domain rules. 2. Use insights to find patterns beyond predefined evaluations Evaluations test the requirements a team already knows how to define. Insights can look across production traces for recurring behavior the team did not anticipate, bring related executions together, and show representative evidence. Custom categories and additional instructions can focus that analysis on business-specific concerns. Developers still review the cited traces and compare the finding with business expectations before deciding that an issue is real. 3. Turn recurring guidance into a reusable skill When a verified issue reflects guidance the agent should apply across many future interactions, repeatedly tuning prompts might not be enough. A versioned skill can capture that learning in a form the team can review, evaluate, and deliberately adopt. Not every issue belongs in a skill. Code defects, tool-description problems, data-quality issues, and platform failures still need to go to the workflow that owns the responsible layer. 4. Compare trade-offs, not only quality scores A candidate can improve one behavior while using more tokens, adding latency, or regressing on normal conversations. Compare candidates with the baseline and inspect the underlying evaluation cases. 5. Keep production changes explicit Continuous analysis can discover new patterns, and optimization can test candidates. Neither should remove the developer's responsibility to review evidence, approve changes, and test the promoted version before sending production traffic to it. The next chapter: keep learning after launch Production is not the end of the evaluation set. It is where new evidence begins. Real users ask questions in ways a development team did not anticipate. Data changes, tools evolve, and a response that works for one scenario can fail at the edge of another. The opportunity is to turn those new production behaviors into the next round of learning without losing the controls that made the launch possible. For Gulf Air and other enterprises building complex agents, that means establishing a repeatable rhythm: Observe new behavior in production traces. Verify the pattern against representative evidence and business expectations. Turn confirmed failures into evaluation coverage. Test candidate changes against the current baseline. Compare quality, latency, and cost rather than optimizing one measure in isolation. Promote a change only after human review, then watch the new version under real traffic. This is the larger promise of continuous improvement in Microsoft Foundry. Insights from production traces can help teams discover what deserves attention. Evaluation makes expected behavior testable. Agent optimizer can compare possible improvements. Developers remain responsible for deciding what is correct, what is safe, and what should reach production. The next milestone is not an agent that changes itself without oversight. It is a controlled learning system in which production evidence, business context, evaluation, and human decisions reinforce one another. For Gulf Air, the first milestone is already real: difficult questions became evidence, evidence became engineering work, and that work helped two agents reach production with greater confidence.

titre: Turn Human Feedback into a Reusable Quality Bar for AI Agents
contenu: Human-in-the-loop for evaluation quality is now in public preview in Microsoft Foundry, announced at Microsoft Ignite on November 17, 2026. Your agent handled 10,000 conversations last week. Your team reviewed 50 and uncovered critical issues. But what happens to those findings? Too often, they end up in a spreadsheet, disconnected from your evaluation pipeline, never becoming reusable tests or measurable quality signals. Production traces reveal how your agent behaves with real users. Human reviewers bring the expertise to identify what worked, what failed, and what the agent should have done differently. The challenge is to turn these human feedbacks into evaluation signals that continuously measure and improve agent quality. With Human-in-the-loop for evaluation quality in Microsoft Foundry, teams can turn real-world agent interactions and human feedback into trusted evaluation datasets, actionable quality signals, and repeatable tests - connecting human judgment directly to the evaluation and optimization loop. Why agent evaluation needs human feedback Automated evaluators make it possible to assess AI agents at scale. But scale is only valuable when you can trust the results. When an LLM judge says your agent passed, is it evaluating what your business actually cares about? Unlike traditional software, good agent behavior is often defined by business requirements, domain expertise, and customer expectations. This knowledge typically lives in review comments, spreadsheets, and people's heads rather than in evaluation workflows. AI Agent teams face three challenges: Valuable test cases are buried in production. Real-world failures, edge cases, and unexpected behaviors are hidden among thousands of traces. Human feedback is difficult to reuse. Reviewer comments explain what went wrong, but cannot directly evaluate a different response from a future agent version. Not every dataset is a trusted benchmark. A large collection of examples doesn't necessarily represent the quality bar a team wants to maintain. What's new Human-in-the-loop addresses these challenges by connecting production behavior, human feedback, evaluation and agent improvement in one workflow. It supports three goals: Goal How Human-in-the-loop helps Build trusted evaluation datasets Convert production traces and conversations into representative test cases with human-reviewed expected outputs and annotations. Make evaluation trustworthy Generate test-case-specific scoring criteria from human feedback and evaluate agent responses against them. Close the improvement loop Reuse trusted datasets and task-level rubric evaluators to identify regressions and measure agent improvements. From production behavior to evaluation datasets Start with traces or conversations from an agent that’s already running. Use trace filters to identify representative scenarios, including successful interactions, recurring failures, and edge cases. For multi-turn tasks, review the full conversation to capture enough context for evaluation. Reviewers can capture four types of feedback directly on traces: Ratings: Overall assessment, such as thumbs up or down. Tags: Categories for scenarios and failure patterns. Comments: Why a response is right or wrong. Expected outputs (ground truth): What the agent should have said or done. Select annotated traces or conversations and add them to a new or existing evaluation dataset. When you enable test-case rubric generation, choose a model deployment. During dataset generation, Foundry preserves annotations and expected outputs, summarize conversations, and generate scoring criteria for an individual test case. Review generated rows and criteria before evaluating so they reflect the right context, policies, and expected behavior. Build a benchmark your team trusts Not all evaluation datasets serve the same purpose. A golden dataset is a small, intentionally curated collection of high-value examples that your team trusts as a benchmark for agent quality. These examples are typically grounded in production behavior and reviewed by domain experts. Unlike broad datasets used for experimentation or testing, golden datasets establish a consistent quality baseline. In Foundry, teams can mark a dataset as golden. Teams should continue reviewing and maintaining these benchmarks as production behavior and business requirements evolve. Keep the improvement loop grounded This is where human feedback becomes a repeatable evaluation signal. Consider a reviewer comment: "Explained how to request a refund but omitted the 30-day deadline." This feedback describes a specific response. But when the agent changes, it may generate a completely different response. How can the original feedback evaluate the new response? Foundry addresses this with task-level rubric evaluators - automatically generating test-case scoring criteria that can be used to evaluate future responses to the same scenario. When adding annotated traces or conversations to a dataset with test-case rubrics generation enabled, teams select a model deployment. Foundry uses conversation history and human annotations to generate scoring criteria for each test case. For example, the reviewer comment can become a reusable criterion: "The response must state that refund requests must be submitted within 30 days." Expected outputs are preserved exactly as written and evaluated separately rather than being paraphrased into rubric criteria. For multi-turn evaluation, Foundry generates a conversation summary describing the scenario represented by each test case. Rubrics are generated during dataset creation, not dynamically during evaluation, so teams can inspect the generated criteria before using them. Teams should still use the shared quality rubric evaluators to consistently apply configured criteria across multiple test cases. The task-level rubric evaluator is a complementary approach for allowing teams to evaluate both scenario-specific requirements and broader quality expectations. To validate whether human feedback improves the effectiveness of rubric-based evaluation, we tested this approach on HelpSteer3, a public dataset of human preference judgments. Rubrics informed by human annotations improved alignment with human preferences from 65% to 81% - a 16-percentage-point gain , approaching the 89% agreement achieved by a second human annotator. By incorporating human feedback into test-case rubric generation, the task-level evaluator became more effective at distinguishing responses that better align with human preferences. These results demonstrate how human expertise can improve the fidelity of automated evaluation to human judgment while generating reusable, task-specific criteria for consistently assessing agent quality. Get started Human-in-the-loop for evaluation connects production traces or conversations, human feedback, curated datasets, and evaluation. It focuses on building agent improvement loop. To get started, you’ll need: A Microsoft Foundry project with an agent that emits traces. Tracing configured with a connected Application Insights resource. Permissions to access traces and create evaluation datasets. A supported region for trace-based data generation. A model deployment (required for test-case rubric generation) Production traces and annotations may contain sensitive information. Review privacy, retention, and dataset-access requirements before creating or sharing evaluation datasets. Try it Now: Follow the step-by-step guide to create your first golden dataset and task-level rubrics from production traces for evaluation [Human in the loop (preview) - Microsoft Foundry | Microsoft Learn ] Watch the Ignite Session: [ From traces to better agents: The Foundry improvement loop ]

titre: Foundry IQ: now managed for you in every Foundry project
contenu: Foundry IQ: Now managed for you in every Foundry project Building AI agents that can answer questions from your documents just got simpler. Today we're announcing that every Microsoft Foundry project will include a managed Foundry IQ resource. Create knowledge bases and ground agents directly from your project, with no separate Foundry IQ (Azure AI Search) service to provision or manage. With a managed Foundry IQ resource, it's easier to connect your agent to a knowledge base and activate market-leading agentic retrieval, ingestion, content security, indexing, and source connections within your Foundry agent-building experience. You choose the content; Foundry IQ manages the underlying grounding infrastructure. Request access to the Foundry Managed Knowledge preview . We're starting with limited preview access and plan to roll out managed Foundry IQ to all Microsoft Foundry projects in December 2026. How it works Start with an eligible project and permissions to create a knowledge base and access the content you want to use. Step 1: Open Knowledge in your Foundry project and select Create a knowledge base . In the configuration pane, use the Managed by Foundry resource and enter a name for your knowledge base. Step 2: Select Upload files to add your files as a knowledge source. Foundry IQ processes the uploaded content and prepares it for retrieval through a searchable index. Once the knowledge source status changes to Active , save the knowledge base. You can also connect a knowledge source supported by the managed preview. For supported file formats, upload limits, and processing details, see Create a file knowledge source . Find evidence across documents with agentic retrieval With model-based query planning enabled, Foundry IQ can break a complex question into focused searches, run them in parallel, and bring the relevant passages together for the agent. For example, asking "How do our Q3 sales in Europe compare with our Q2 forecast?" may require retrieving actual sales results, forecast assumptions, and regional performance data from different documents. Foundry IQ can plan and execute focused searches across those sources to gather the evidence needed for a grounded response. Source references let users check where the answer came from. Learn how agentic retrieval works . Use microsoft-retriever-1 out of the box for fast, low-cost retrieval, or bring your own supported model to tune the trade-off between latency, cost, and answer quality. Different workloads may benefit from different models depending on query complexity, retrieval requirements, and performance goals. Ground your agent and test its answers From the saved knowledge base, select Add to an agent . In the agent playground, ask a question that draws on multiple files and open a citation to check that the source supports the answer. Then try a question answered by one document and another the documents can't answer. For the latter, check that the agent acknowledges the gap. Choose how to run Foundry IQ Use a managed Foundry IQ resource when you want to create a knowledge base in your project and have Foundry manage the search infrastructure. Bring your own Foundry IQ (Azure AI Search) resource when you want to reuse existing search indexes or indexing pipelines, define custom index schemas, or control the search resource configuration directly. Supported knowledge sources and configuration options vary by setup. Get started Request access to private preview and try grounding an agent with a set of documents you know well. titre: External agents in Microsoft Foundry are now generally available
contenu:
Built your agent somewhere else? Foundry can still help you measure and improve it. External agents in Microsoft Foundry are now generally available. If your agent runs outside Foundry and sends OpenTelemetry traces to Application Insights, you can register it in Foundry and use those traces to observe and evaluate it, without moving or rebuilding the agent. Registration, the agent trace view, Agent Insights, and continuous evaluation of production traces are generally available. Other capabilities in this post are in preview and are labeled where they appear. Why use production traces? Because they show you what your tests missed. Take Contoso Travel, a fictional company that runs its own trip-planning agent outside Foundry.* Before launch, the agent passed every test the team wrote. After launch, users asked about carry-on bag rules and planned trips with three or four cities. Neither was in the test set. That's normal: tests cover the scenarios your team thought of, and real users bring the rest. This post follows Contoso as they connect the agent to Foundry, find problems in production, turn expert review into tests, and use those tests to measure and improve the agent. Connect the agent you already have Your agent keeps running where it is, on its existing endpoint. You send its traces to Application Insights, register it in Foundry, and Foundry reads the traces from there. Before you begin , you need: An Application Insights resource connected to your Foundry project. An agent that emits OpenTelemetry traces following the GenAI semantic conventions , with a gen_ai.agent.id attribute on its invoke_agent span . Agents built with frameworks other than the one shown here can also connect if they emit compatible traces. The Foundry User role on the project, and Monitoring Reader on the Application Insights resource to view traces. For the full list of prerequisites, see Register external agents for observability and evaluation . Contoso's agent is built with Microsoft Agent Framework in Python and runs on Azure Kubernetes Service. Connecting it takes three steps. Step 1: Send traces to Application Insights import os

from agent_framework import Agent
from agent_framework.openai import OpenAIChatCompletionClient
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from microsoft.opentelemetry import use_microsoft_opentelemetry

# Send traces, including prompts and responses, to Application Insights.
use_microsoft_opentelemetry(
    enable_azure_monitor=True,
    azure_monitor_connection_string=os.environ["APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING"],
    enable_sensitive_data=True,
)

client = OpenAIChatCompletionClient(
    model=os.environ["AZURE_OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT"],
    azure_endpoint=os.environ["AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT"],
    credential=DefaultAzureCredential(),
)

agent = Agent(
    client,
    "You are Contoso Travel's trip-planning assistant...",
    id="contoso-trip-planner",  # Emitted as gen_ai.agent.id. Register the agent with this ID in step 2.
    name="contoso-trip-planner",
    tools=[search_flights, search_hotels, policy_lookup],
) This uses the Microsoft OpenTelemetry distro . Call use_microsoft_opentelemetry once at startup, before you create the agent. Decide early how you'll handle message content. enable_sensitive_data=True records prompts and responses in your traces. Evaluators that score what the agent said, such as quality and rubric evaluators, need that content. The tracing docs recommend turning content recording off in production unless you need it. Before you turn it on in production, decide what content you're allowed to capture, who can see it, how long you keep it, and whether to redact it first. For the full set of considerations, see Restrict access to sensitive content in Microsoft Foundry traces and Tracing and data handling . Step 2: Register the agent in Foundry In the Foundry portal , go to Build > Agents > New agent > Link external agent , then enter the agent name and its OpenTelemetry ID. Or use the SDK (azure-ai-projects 2.11.0 or later): import os
from azure.ai.projects import AIProjectClient
from azure.ai.projects.models import ExternalAgentDefinition
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

project = AIProjectClient(
    endpoint=os.environ["FOUNDRY_PROJECT_ENDPOINT"],
    credential=DefaultAzureCredential(),
)

project.agents.create_version(
    agent_name="contoso-trip-planner",
    definition=ExternalAgentDefinition(otel_agent_id="contoso-trip-planner"),
) Step 3: Check that traces arrive Send the agent a few requests, then open the agent's Traces tab in Foundry. Traces usually appear within a few minutes. If traces don't show up, see Troubleshoot missing traces . That's the setup. The rest of this post builds on those traces, and you can adopt each part on its own. Find problems in production With traces flowing, the next step is finding what's going wrong. Once an agent is live, there are too many conversations to read one by one, and bad answers often don't show up as errors in logs. Start with the trace view. Filter by time range, status, or token count to narrow down the traces you want to review, then open a run. The trace view shows each run step by step, based on what your traces record, such as model calls, tool calls with their inputs and outputs, and messages. That context can help you investigate where a run went wrong, rather than seeing only the final result. For a deeper look across many traces, use Agent Insights . You can run it on demand or periodically. It analyzes the agent's recent traces with a model you choose, then groups recurring issues and shows each one with its severity, the linked traces, and a proposed next step. Foundry doesn't have access to an external agent's code, so for external agents that proposal is general guidance for you to apply in your own code. Changing an insight's status records your decision. It doesn't change your agent. Contoso's Agent Insights run flagged a recurring multi-city issue: the agent searched every pair of cities and then searched the same legs again. Around the same time, the support team saw complaints about carry-on answers. Filtering the traces to bag questions showed the agent quoting a size limit that was out of date. It answered from its instructions and never called policy_lookup , the tool that returns the current policy. Instead of reading traces one by one, the team used these signals to decide which traces to look at closely. Turn human expert review into reusable tests Agent Insights shows you where to look. Deciding whether an answer is actually wrong often takes someone who knows the business. An LLM judge can help score whether an answer is relevant and grounded, but a general-purpose LLM judge may not know that your airline partner changed its bag rules last month. Your domain experts do, but their judgment often ends up in a chat thread or a support ticket and doesn't make it back into testing. In Foundry, a human expert's review can become a test you re-run. Foundry calls this human in the loop . Annotate the trace (preview). Reviewers can rate a run, add tags, leave a comment, and write the answer they expected. Contoso's support lead reviewed the carry-on traces, marked them as incorrect, and wrote the expected answer with the current limit. The support lead did the same for a few multi-city trips. One useful practice, also recommended in the annotation docs , is to annotate good runs as well as bad ones, and to say in the comment why an answer is wrong. A score alone doesn't record the reason. Turn annotations into test cases. Foundry can generate dataset rows from annotated traces. A generated row keeps the user's question and the reviewer's expected answer, and Foundry can add a task-level rubric (preview): pass/fail criteria for that specific case. For a carry-on question, one criterion checks that the agent calls policy_lookup before giving a bag rule. The team reviewed the rows, edited one that was too strict, and added them to their golden dataset: a small, reviewed set of test cases the team trusts and re-runs to compare agent versions. Define shared quality criteria. Task-level rubrics check specific scenarios. A shared rubric applies the same criteria across an evaluation. Foundry can generate one from a description of the agent's job that you write, plus its production traces, and the team edits it to match their standards. Contoso added a criterion that policy answers must come from policy_lookup , so the carry-on lesson applies to fees and seat rules too. When they regenerate the rubric later, Foundry keeps the dimensions they edited and the version history. As a result, the support lead's judgment is captured in evaluation artifacts the team can reuse, and the tests come from questions users actually asked. Measure and improve With a golden dataset and a shared rubric, Contoso can measure the agent the same way every time. That matters because quality can change after launch, for example when a tool's data changes or someone edits a prompt. To know whether a change helped, you need to measure the same way before and after. You can also evaluate the agent continuously. Foundry scores a sample of its production traces at an interval you set, such as every hour. Intelligent sampling picks a varied set of traces rather than a random one. Use the shared rubric, built-in evaluators, or your own custom evaluators. Contoso added a custom evaluator that checks each answer against the current policy, the kind of fact a general-purpose judge wouldn't know. Each scheduled run records its scores, so you can track quality over time and set an alert in Azure Monitor when a score falls . Low scores are also a good place to look for the next traces to annotate. With the problems identified, the team had two ways to improve the agent. Fix it yourself. For carry-on bags, the cause was clear. The team updated the instructions to always call policy_lookup for bag and fee questions, then re-ran the golden dataset. In this example, the carry-on rows passed and the other rows still passed. Learn from past traces with skill optimization (preview). Multi-city trips were harder to fix by hand, so the team tried skill optimization. It analyzes past traces, along with any annotations and evaluation results, and proposes a new or updated skill: a versioned folder of instructions, with a SKILL.md file and optional scripts and reference files, that an agent can load when it needs them. The team ran it on recent traces with a focus on multi-city planning. It returned findings and a proposed skill. A successful run means the run finished. It doesn't mean the proposal is better. The team reviewed the findings and the proposed skill before trying it. Because the agent runs outside Foundry, they downloaded the skill into the agent's project, then re-ran the golden dataset to compare it with the current version. A skill ships only if the comparison shows it helps. Either way, the check is the same: run the same golden dataset before and after and compare. Put it together Each piece works on its own, and they also connect into one loop. Here's the carry-on issue from start to finish: Detect: support complaints and a trace filter surface outdated carry-on answers. Review: the support lead marks the traces incorrect and writes the expected answer. Test: the annotated traces become rows in the golden dataset. Fix and re-run: the team updates the instructions and re-runs the golden dataset. Ship and monitor: Foundry continuously evaluates a sample of production traffic. Steps 1 to 4 fix the issue in front of you. Over time, the team adds reviewed cases to the golden dataset and refines the shared rubric, so later evaluations include what they learned earlier. Pre-launch testing still matters. Production can add scenarios those tests missed, including unexpected requests or misuse, and expert review helps you decide which ones should become test cases. Start where you are You don't need everything at once. Start at the top and go as far as you need: Stage What to do Connect Link your agent and check its traces Learn Filter and review traces, run Agent Insights, and annotate traces that show the problems your team cares about Capture Build a golden dataset and define evaluation criteria Measure Continuously evaluate a sample of production traces Improve Test each proposed change against the same golden dataset Get started Register your external agent , send it a few requests, and open its Traces tab. To try the full workflow, start from our external agent sample. titre: The designs we didn't ship: How user feedback shaped the new Teams meeting controls
contenu: Some of the most important product decisions we've made weren't about what to ship. They were about what not to ship. When we began rethinking the meeting controls in Microsoft Teams, the challenge was clear. Meetings had become more capable, and the interface had grown along with them. As Teams meetings became more capable, we saw an opportunity to make controls simpler to navigate and easier to adapt to different meeting needs. And simply adding another button every time Teams gained a capability wasn’t the experience we wanted to carry forward. So we started with a question: Could we make meeting controls simpler today while creating room for Teams to become more capable tomorrow? It took more than one attempt to answer it. First idea: Spread things out An early concept divided the controls across more of the meeting window. The idea made sense on paper: reduce crowding, establish clearer groups, and create additional separation between actions such as Share and Leave. Initial research gave us reasons to keep exploring it. Participants responded positively to aspects of the cleaner layout and clearer grouping. But repeated use revealed tradeoffs. In our first longitudinal study, supplemented by feedback from early users and customer sessions, we identified tradeoffs in control placement, discoverability, and Leave separation that informed the next iteration. It looked cleaner. But looking cleaner wasn't enough. A meeting toolbar isn't something people simply look at. It's something they operate quickly while concentrating on a conversation, presentation, or task. So we kept going. Next, we tested very different answers Instead of debating design philosophies, we decided to test them. We developed three approaches: All centered: Put controls together in one predictable place. Three columns: Separate families of controls and use more of the available screen. Cleaned-up current: Reduce clutter while preserving more of the familiar structure. We gave those experiences to for a large cohort for a month, with participants responding to surveys twice a week. We looked at signals including findability, efficiency, confidence, effort, satisfaction, and perceived value. Just as importantly, we looked at how participants' reactions developed as they became familiar with each design. The findings exposed an important tradeoff. The lesson wasn't simply that one design had "won." It was that visual simplicity and operational simplicity aren't necessarily the same thing. Then users challenged the idea of a perfect toolbar We had been approaching the toolbar partly as an optimization problem: determine which controls belong there, identify the best order, and create the right default. What we learned from participants led us to reconsider that assumption. People use Teams differently. A presenter may have different priorities from someone participating in a large group discussion. Someone who records frequently may want Record immediately accessible. Another person may prioritize Notes, Copilot, People, reactions, or something else. Across the research, we heard a clear desire for more control over that experience. Let me customize it. That changed our thinking. Instead of trying to create one perfect toolbar, we focused on creating a system people could adapt. Pin. Unpin. Rearrange. Bring forward the controls that matter to you. The goal became a simpler starting point without assuming that everyone's definition of "simple" is the same. Finding the problems that still remained By early 2026, the design had converged substantially. But before expanding the rollout, we conducted a structured review around nine meeting tasks. Could participants mute? Add and remove controls? Take notes? Raise their hand? Record? Start transcription without recording? That final task exposed an issue we needed to fix. The capability existed, but some participants weren't reliably finding or understanding it. That's an important distinction in product design: A capability delivers the most value when people can easily discover and use it. The review surfaced other opportunities too. Relying on right-click wasn't enough to make customization discoverable for everyone, and the difference between temporary and permanently pinned controls needed to be clearer. So we iterated again. Listening to more than one signal There wasn't a single metric that could tell us whether we had the design right. We combined what people told us through research and surveys with aggregated product usage insights. We looked at questions such as whether participants could find what they needed, how confident they felt, and how they perceived different designs. We also examined how early users interacted with controls and menus, and we listened closely to people who chose to return to the previous experience during testing. When someone told us a control was difficult to find, an interaction took too long, or a change disrupted something familiar, that feedback helped us understand where the design still needed work. Predictability matters As more people tried the experience, their preferences weren't always the same. Some participants wanted Raise hand visible at all times. Others liked its association with reactions. Some preferred fewer visible controls. Others wanted to make fuller use of a large display. Some appreciated additional separation between Leave and Share. Others noticed even small changes to locations they knew well. One particularly useful lesson came from feedback about dynamic controls. A toolbar can become harder to operate when controls move unexpectedly during an interaction. That reinforced a design principle that stayed with us: Simplicity isn't only about reducing clutter. It's also about predictability. People in meetings have better things to think about than where their interface went. Where we landed After the prototypes, longitudinal research, surveys, experience reviews, telemetry, card sorting, diary studies, and a lot of iteration, the principles behind the final direction became relatively straightforward: Keep frequently needed actions accessible. Separate Leave from common controls. Make the broader toolbox easier to navigate. Let people personalize their controls. And build an information architecture with room to evolve. The finished experience can make those decisions seem obvious. What you don't see are the designs that didn't survive the research. That's the part of this work I'm most proud of. We didn't need to have the right answer on the first try because we built a process that allowed users to help us find a better one. Shipping is another beginning The new Microsoft Teams meeting controls are becoming broadly available. Learn more about how to set up and use . That gives us something our prototypes and studies couldn't: feedback from a much broader range of real-world meetings and ways of working. So if you've tried the new controls, tell us what you think in the blog comments. What did we get right? What could we make even better? And what's the next thing we should simplify? Some of the most valuable moments in this journey began when user feedback challenged our assumptions. We're still listening.

titre: The GitHub app in Microsoft Teams is now generally available!
contenu: GitHub empowers any team to become builders in Microsoft Teams. Customer support teams are using GitHub to turn customer feedback from Teams channels into filed issues. Engineering teams are asking GitHub to investigate, reproduce, and fix bugs without leaving Teams. Business and marketing teams with innovative ideas are asking GitHub to turn their discussions into working prototypes. During public preview, our team has been hard at work addressing feedback and making product improvements to the GitHub experience in Teams. Here is what’s new. Review work in the GitHub Canvas The new GitHub canvas lets you review the plan, file changes, and pull request without leaving Teams. Click “Open Canvas” to follow GitHub Copilot’s progress and see your team’s ideas take shape in code, right beside the conversation. Go from notification to pull request in one app GitHub notifications and GitHub Copilot now live in a single app in Teams called GitHub. Stay on top of issue and pull request updates and act on them right in Teams. When an update needs attention, reply to the notification with "@GitHub". GitHub Copilot can investigate, make the fix, and draft a pull request in the same thread, so your team sees the update and the response together. Issues and pull requests created from Teams now carry attribution. Reviewers can see who started the work and link back to the Teams conversation where it was discussed. Work across repositories and tools Real work rarely lives in one repository. With multi-repo support, GitHub Copilot can work across all the repositories your task needs in the same conversation. In addition, MCP support lets you configure which tools and connected services GitHub can leverage in Teams. Learn more about configuring MCP . Get set up in a guided experience The new guided web onboarding experience helps you sign in through your default browser using saved passwords or passkeys and grant Teams access to the right organizations and repositories. You can now use natural language to ask GitHub to use a default repository or switch repositories in your Teams conversations. You can also choose the model GitHub Copilot uses for a task. Pick a faster model for quick fixes or a more capable model for larger changes. Get started today Add the GitHub app to Teams today, then click “Get started” from its welcome message to connect your account. Type "@GitHub help" to see what else it can do. Admins should verify the following are enabled for users to get started: Microsoft 365 admins: ensure resource-specific consent is enabled so users can let the GitHub app use conversation context. TAC admins: ensure the GitHub app is allowed for users in the Teams admin center. GitHub enterprise admins: ensure Copilot cloud agent, cloud sandboxes , and CLI billing are enabled for each organization and assign GitHub Copilot licenses to users. Learn more at teams.github.com ! We'd love to hear what you build. Share your feedback in the comments below.

titre: Turn GitHub notifications into code with GitHub Copilot in Microsoft Teams
contenu: GitHub can now bring repository updates into a channel, group chat, or private chat. When an update needs action, reply to the notification and @mention GitHub with the task you want GitHub Copilot to carry out. GitHub Copilot uses the issue or pull request linked in the notification and the conversation in the thread to understand the task. It can reproduce a bug, run tests, implement a fix, and prepare a pull request for review. Turn an issue notification into a pull request If the player doesn’t load, open the video in a new window: Open video For a bug report, the workflow starts in the notification thread: A GitHub Issue notification arrives in a Teams channel with a link to the reported bug. You @mention GitHub to investigate the issue and prepare a proposed fix in a pull request. The team reviews the pull request, iterates with GitHub Copilot, tests the proposed changes, and decides whether to merge. Starting from the linked issue and thread lets your team delegate the work to GitHub Copilot without rebuilding the request from scratch. The same workflow can be used to implement a feature, expand test coverage, update documentation, and more. Product and engineering teams at Microsoft are already leveraging the GitHub app in Teams to build products today. Get started Explore the new GitHub app in Microsoft Teams (previously called GitHub Notifications). If you already have GitHub Notifications installed, update the app to the latest version. The legacy GitHub app will be renamed “GitHub (deprecated)” and retired on November 16. Learn more at teams.github.com ! Turn the updates your team follows into code your team can review.

titre: Making Microsoft Teams more responsive, reliable, and ready for work
contenu: By: Ihor Lukyanenko, Harsh Nagaonkar, Vishal Ratna and Suprem Gupta Every day, people rely on Microsoft Teams to connect with colleagues, share ideas, make decisions, and move work forward. Whether they're joining a meeting from a laptop, catching up on conversations from a mobile device, or collaborating across multiple projects throughout the day, they expect Teams to be fast, responsive, and ready when they need it. In our June 202 6 update , we shared gains across chat switching, reduced hangs and freezes, and faster people search. Since then, we’ve continued to raise the bar. From hardware-constrained devices to employees working on the go from mobile phones, delivering a consistent, high-quality experience across every platform remains a key focus for the Teams engineering team. In this post, we'll highlight several recent performance investments that are helping make Teams faster, more efficient, and more responsive across desktop and mobile experiences. Performance improvements at a glance T eams Efficiency Mode: Delivering a Better Experience on Hardware-Constrained Devices | Windows, MacOS Great collaboration experiences shouldn't depend on having the latest hardware. Many of our customers rely on older devices, entry-level laptops, or systems operating under challenging network constraints. As organizations extend device lifecycles and support increasingly diverse hardware fleets, ensuring a high-quality of experience across all configurations remains an important priority. This is why in June we launched Teams Efficiency Mode, a set of optimizations designed to reduce resource consumption and improve overall responsiveness on hardware-constrained devices. Teams Efficiency Mode gets enabled by default on devices with slower / legacy CPUs and limited amount of RAM (8GB or less). Users on such devices see a corresponding indicator in the Teams title bar. Also, on any device, Efficiency Mode can be turned on and off manually through the dedicated setting. The benefits are visible in everyday workflows. In Efficiency Mode, Teams launches up to 20% faster on hardware-constrained devices , helping users get into conversations, meetings, and tasks more quickly. When in a meeting, Teams automatically adjusts the resolution of user’s camera to preserve the CPU headroom for the audio path. As a result, users on hardware-constrained devices can maintain a high quality of their meeting experience despite the disproportionately higher thermal throttling rates. Encouraged by these early wins, we are actively working on expanding the set of optimizations applied in Efficiency Mode. By making Teams more efficient and resilient on a wider range of hardware, we're helping ensure that users can stay productive, collaborate confidently, and get the most out of Teams regardless of the device they're using. Making Responsive ness Measurable – and Actionable | Android Responsiveness has consistently been one of the biggest sources of dissatisfaction in our Android customers’ feedback. We knew users were experiencing friction, but we lacked a single metric that could measure responsiveness across the many interactions they perform every day. To close that gap, we introduced the App Responsiveness Index (ARI). ARI connects real user actions—such as taps, scrolling, and navigation—with Android frame data. It groups frames into roughly 208 ms “blinks” and measures the perceived smoothness of each interaction and screen. More importantly, it gives teams actionable telemetry at the individual screen level. That visibility made the main causes of poor responsiveness much clearer: Memory issues, responsible for approximately 60–65% of the impact Blocking work on the main thread Heavy layouts We started by addressing memory horizontally across the app. This included fixing memory leaks, reducing database-call explosions, and resolving out-of-memory failures. The results were significant. Our slow-frame metric improved 40% YoY. We also brought the user-perceived ANR rate down to an all-time low of 0.12%. Targeted memory improvements reduced total blocking garbage-collection duration by 23% . Because blocking GC pauses application work, this improvement has a direct effect on how responsive the app feels. We also wanted to make these gains sustainable. For scenarios covered by system tests, we introduced memory regression gates that evaluate changes before they are merged. These gates have already caught several potential regressions at the pull-request stage. In parallel, we built AI-powered pull-request guardrails to identify risky patterns even earlier. These guardrails currently operate at 93% precision , and we are evolving them into an agentic system that can detect, explain, and eventually help prevent responsiveness regressions before they reach production. Image Thumbnails – 17% Faster Loading | Android Every day, people use Microsoft Teams to share screenshots, photos, files, and other visual context that keeps work moving. In media-heavy chats and channels, those images are often experienced first as thumbnails while users scroll through a conversation. When those thumbnails appear late, the conversation can feel less responsive even when the service behind it is healthy. Making media-heavy chats feel smoother For users, the problem was simple: in some Android conversations, thumbnails did not always keep pace with scrolling. A user could reach a message and briefly see an empty placeholder before the image appeared. In other cases, multiple thumbnails appeared together after a delay, creating a bursty experience that made scrolling feel uneven. This was especially visible in chats and channels with a lot of shared media. Images are part of the conversation, so delays in rendering them interrupt the flow of reading, reviewing, and responding. The goal of this work was to make thumbnails appear earlier and more predictably as users move through a conversation. The interesting part was that the backend was not the whole story. Service-side latency could look healthy, and many images were already being served from cache. Still, the user could see delayed thumbnails. That told us we needed to look at the full client-side journey of an image, not just request and response timing. How we did it: mapping the image journey To understand the gap, the team created Image Journey Mapper for Android. This was not a feature by itself; it was a diagnostic subsystem designed to answer one question: where does time go between creating a media block and showing the thumbnail on screen? We first identified the milestones that mattered in the lifecycle of a thumbnail: UI block creation, view attachment, cache lookup, network queueing, download, decode, and render. Then we added instrumentation across those stages and flighted the diagnostic code only to Canary users, which are Microsoft internal users. That allowed us to collect real usage data while keeping the scope controlled. For this investigation, the journey events were written into a separate purpose-built table in the device database. Once enough data was collected from internal users viewing images in Teams, the team analyzed the patterns across many journeys. The important shift was that image rendering was no longer a single opaque interval; it became a stage-by-stage timeline. What we found The Journey Mapper data surfaced three important client-side bottlenecks. They were valuable because each one pointed to a different layer of the image pipeline, and each required a different kind of fix. 1. Some images were being fetched again after cache churn In media-heavy sessions, larger thumbnails and smaller frequently reused assets could compete for cache space. When smaller assets were evicted, the app had to fetch them again even though they were likely to be needed repeatedly. The fix was to make cache behavior more intentional by separating workloads so smaller frequently reused images were less likely to be displaced by larger media. 2. Some requests were waiting in the client network queue A slow thumbnail can look like a network problem from high-level telemetry. The mapped journey showed a more specific pattern: for some images, transfer had not started yet. The request was waiting in the client networking layer. That led us to tune network concurrency for image-heavy workloads so independent thumbnail requests could make better use of available device and network capacity. 3. Loading often started too close to display time The mapper also showed that image blocks could exist before their thumbnails started loading. That meant the app had unused time before the user reached the image. To take advantage of that window, we introduced thumbnail warmup: upcoming media blocks near the viewport can be prepared before they are visible, with cache-aware checks and bounded concurrency. What we changed The fixes followed the diagnosis. We tuned the networking path for concurrent image requests, made cache behavior more predictable for different image sizes and reuse patterns, and added controlled thumbnail warmup so images could be prepared before the user reached them. These changes were designed to improve perceived performance without turning prefetch into unbounded background work. Warmup remains cache-aware, concurrency is limited, and rollout is measured carefully so latency gains are balanced with responsiveness, device resource usage, and reliability. What we have seen so far This work is still in progress. The experience has been validated in internal rings and exposed to our private preview customers for a meaningful period. The team is using the learnings from that exposure to prepare the next broader rollout phase, with general availability as the near-term goal. The current results show that the targeted image-pipeline changes are moving the experience in the right direction, with a measured latency reduction of approximately 17%. More importantly, the visible user impact is clearer in day-to-day use: thumbnails are pre-loaded before the user reaches them, loaders are no longer visible in the optimized path, and users do not have to pause for images to load while scrolling through media-heavy conversations. At the same time, we continue to carefully observe the rollout to ensure that latency gains are balanced with responsiveness, device resource usage, and reliability. Looking Forward As Microsoft Teams continues to evolve with richer collaboration experiences and increasingly intelligent AI-powered capabilities, maintaining a fast and responsive user experience remains a foundational engineering priority. We will continue investing across desktop and mobile platforms to improve responsiveness, reduce resource consumption, accelerate content loading, and ensure Teams performs reliably across the wide range of devices and environments our customers depend on every day.

titre: Cross-Platform Meeting Connect: Great in-room meeting experiences across Teams and Zoom
contenu: Your team is gathered in a Teams Room for a project review, but the customer’s invitation is for a Zoom meeting. You want to use the room’s audio, video, and displays, share the presentation, and stay connected to the conversation. You shouldn’t have to give up your room’s setup just because the meeting is on another platform. Whether your organization uses Teams or Zoom Meetings today, people need the flexibility to meet with customers, partners, and colleagues on a range of platforms. Direct Guest Join will allow Teams Rooms to join Zoom Meetings and Zoom Rooms to join Teams meetings. Microsoft and Zoom are building on that foundation with Cross-Platform Meeting Connect , to address some of the most requested needs of people joining meetings from a conference room, regardless of the platform they use. The goal is a more complete room experience for the everyday cross-platform meetings that bring organizations together. Planned improvements to sharing, meeting visibility, room controls, and HD video are designed to help people contribute confidently using the room’s capabilities. Share ideas from the room A more seamless room experience also means making it easy to share and view content. With planned HDMI sharing, people will be able to connect a laptop to the room and share content directly into the meeting. The room will also be able to display content shared by oth er participants, helping everyone follow the same presentation or document. Stay connected to people and the conversation Knowing who is in the meeting helps people collaborate with confidence. A participant roster is designed to show the meeting participant list on room display and update as people join and leave. It will give in-room participants a clearer view of who is in the meeting especially when some attendees are not visible in the current video layout. Enhanced chat visibility will help everyone in the room follow both parts of the meeting conversation by bringing read-only chat into the room layout alongside the meeting video. People will be able to show or hide the chat panel as needed, without having chat appear unexpectedly over video. This experience is read-only: participants will be able to view chat supplied by the meeting platform but not compose or send messages from the room itself. Use familiar room controls People should be able to rely on the controls in front of them. With Cross-Platform Meeting Connect, planned improvements will keep room hardware and touch console controls synced with the hosted meeting, prioritizing mute, unmute, and end-call for the initial delivery. That synchronization is intended to preserve the room's behavior people expect and reduce uncertainty about whether the room is muted or has left the call. Keep people and content in view For rooms with two displays, we are introducing a layout that uses each screen for a different purpose: shared content on one screen and the participant gallery on the other. This would let in-room attendees follow a presentation while keeping remote participants in view. Video improvements support sending and receiving video at up to 1080p for Teams meeting on Zoom Rooms. Actual resolution will depend on the meeting platform’s policies, the room device, and network conditions. The experience is designed to adapt when bandwidth is constrained, or hardware cannot sustain the higher resolution, with meeting reliability remaining a priority. More flexibility, with clear expectations Microsoft and Zoom share a goal of helping people collaborate across platforms while making better use of their meeting rooms. These improvements are designed for both directions, with a focus on the capabilities people need most in everyday room meetings. A guest meeting will still differ from a native meeting, and this work does not extend every enhancement to every platform. As the integration evolves, cross-platform meeting experiences will move forward together. Individual capabilities will depend on support from both the room system and the meeting platform, helping ensure people see controls that work for their meeting experience. What’s next With Cross-Platform Meeting Connect, Teams Rooms will make it easier for people to join, participate, and collaborate in meetings hosted on other platforms, helping organizations get more from their meeting room experience. Stay tuned as we continue working toward more ways to make cross-platform meetings easier and more connected.

titre: What's New in Microsoft Teams | August - September 2026
contenu: A quick note before we get into it: What's New in Teams is shifting from a monthly to a quarterly rhythm. You'll hear from us next in December, March, and June, and each edition will round up everything announced and released over the full quarter. One post, one fuller view of what's new. Two investments shape where Teams is heading, and you'll see both in this quarter's releases: AI transforming teamwork with agents as part of the team, and a simpler, smarter, more secure foundation underneath it all. AI in Teams is showing up in the flow of your work. Teams Phone Agent brings that to your phone line, helping callers with common requests in more than 60 languages and routing them with context attached, so a missed call turns into a next step instead of a lost one. Context carries forward, too. Video recap turns a meeting you missed into a short, narrated highlight reel, so what a meeting decided outlasts the conversation itself. And protection for everyday collaboration is always top of mind. The new Security Detection Report brings detections such as impersonation and malicious URLs into one view in the Teams admin center, so admins see the whole picture in one place. Read on for all the latest updates! Feature categories: (All features listed are generally available unless otherwise noted) Chat and Collaboration Meetings Teams Phone Workplace Teams Events Fundamentals and Security Teams Platform Certified devices Chat and Collaboration Ask Copilot in Teams conversations Stay in the flow of work and get help from Copilot directly within your conversations. Open Copilot from a message or selected text in a Teams conversation, with the relevant context already included, making it easier to gain insights, explore questions, and move work forward without needing to re-explain information. Find a gents and apps faster through Teams search Discover the tools you need with agents and apps surfaced directly in Teams search results. As you type in the search bar, matching agents and apps appear alongside other relevant results, helping you spend less time searching and more time getting things done. Find and share files faster in Teams Locate the files you need while sharing content in Teams. Search for cloud-based files directly from the attachment experience, making it easier to find and share the right content without interrupting the flow of collaboration. Emoji shortcuts on iOS and Android Express yourself with emoji shortcuts. Desktop emoji shortcuts now work on iOS and Android. Insert emojis directly in the compose box by typing a word between colons, so :smile: becomes ðŸ˜Š. Autocomplete suggestions help speed up entry, and custom emojis are also supported. Clearer text highlighting in dark mode and high contrast mode Make highlighted text easier to read while composing messages in Teams. Improvements to text highlighting in dark mode and high contrast mode provide a more consistent and accessible editing experience, helping content stand out more clearly. Meetings Video recap in Teams Meeting recap now delivers a bite-sized video recap of with key highlights from your Teams meeting. It combines AI-generated voiceover summaries with video snippets, spotlighting the most important moments while preserving the original tone and flow, so you can catch up on key topics in a few minutes. Video recaps now support meetings in 23 languages across 31 regional variants, learn more . Translation button to change the language for intelligent meeting recaps After an intelligent meeting recap is generated, you can change the recap language at any time using a translation button, even if a different language was selected during the meeting. Multilingual teams get more flexibility to read meeting insights, action items, and discussion summaries in the language that is most comfortable for them. Redesigned meeting controls Stay focused on your conversations with a customizable meeting toolbar that keeps the controls you need within easy reach. Pin your most-used controls, unpin those you don’t need, and drag and drop them into the order that works for you. Raise Hand now lives inside the React button, while Leave has its own spot on the right to help avoid accidental exits. Teams Phone Teams Phone Agent Teams Phone Agent is an AI-powered receptionist for your business’s phone line, so callers can get help with common requests even after hours. For customer-facing organizations and departments using Teams Phone, such as bank branches or IT help desks, it takes repetitive calls off employees' plates so they can focus on the conversations that truly need a human touch. With support for over 60 languages and locales, Teams Phone Agent handles common requests such as answering routine questions or booking appointments. , And it can route a caller to the right department or employee with an AI-generated summary of the conversation, so customers do not have to navigate phone menus or repeat themselves. Custom voice agents are available for specialized workflows. Teams Phone Agent is now generally available, learn more . If the player doesn’t load, open the video in a new window: Open video Intelligent call recap in Queues app Intelligent call recaps in Queues app help you catch up on recorded or transcribed queue calls with AI-generated summary notes covering key discussion points and follow-up actions. To open a recap, find the call record in the Queues app call history and select Recap. Copilot in Queues app’s shared call history for post-call insights Quickly catch up on a call queue call and uncover key details with the ability to use Copilot in the shared call history in Queues app . After a recorded call is completed, users with Copilot can now open the call record in the shared call history, access the Copilot Chat sidecar from the Recap tab, and ask questions about the call. Automatic recording and transcription for call queues Capture customer interactions without requiring your organization’s calling representatives to manually start recording. Admins can enable automatic recording and transcription for individual Teams c all q ueues and control access to recordings. Recordings are stored in SharePoint and accessible through call recaps in the shared call history in Queues app. View and manage auto attendant shared voicemails in Queues app Help your team stay on top of customer messages by managing auto attendant shared voicemails directly in Queues app. Calls routed from an auto attendant to voicemail will appear in Queues app, giving collaborative calling teams a centralized place to track, triage, and respond to messages. Customize recording and transcription notifications for Teams calls Give your organization greater control over how recording and transcription are communicated during Teams calls. IT admins can customize select user notification strings for recording and transcription in the Teams admin center, helping tailor the experience for participants in Teams VoIP calls. Enhance control of delegated calls with call lock and delegate join alerts Call delegation in Teams gains real controls: a delegator can lock an active call and see when a delegate joins. Locking prevents delegates from joining or resuming the call, and optional warning tones notify participants when a delegate joins or resumes. Workplace Interpreter agent support in Teams Rooms on Android The Interpreter agent acts as a translator in Microsoft Teams meetings, letting participants listen in their chosen language with real-time translation. It is now available in Teams Rooms on Android licensed for Teams Rooms Pro. New room optimization mode in Teams desktop Room optimization mode makes it easier to use your laptop for meetings and collaboration in spaces such as focus or huddle rooms that do not yet have a Teams Rooms system. It replaces shared display mode, has a new location, and enables or disables room-specific features. When room peripherals are connected, Teams can automatically select audio and video devices, enable speaker recognition and shared display, and disable voice isolation. Modernized Gallery view in Teams Rooms on Android The updated Gallery view in Teams Rooms on Android prioritizes video on the meeting stage, arranges participants in consistent aspect ratios, and minimizes movement of participant tiles on stage. You can hide the room self-preview video and choose to see audio and video participants equally on stage instead of prioritizing video participants. Admins can set the default behavior using local device settings and the Pro Management portal. Teams Events Breakout rooms in Teams Meetings & Events Breakout rooms are now supported in Teams Meetings & Teams Events with up to 1,000 participants across 100 rooms, increased from the previous limit of 300 participants across 50 rooms. Organizers can use breakout rooms to create smaller focused sessions within an event for more interaction and collaboration. Specify who has control of production tools in Teams Events Organizers can designate who controls production tools, granting chosen people access to Manage what attendees see and the green room so event production stays with the right crew. The setting is a new meeting option applied when the event is set up. Expanding presenter visibility in “Manage what attendees see” Producers can resize and expand the presenter panel in Manage what attendees see, making it easier to view, manage, and switch between presenters while a live event is running. New layout when sharing content for Teams events Organizers and presenters who have access to production tools now see updated layout options when sharing content in the “Manage what attendees see” experience for Teams events. The available layouts are speaker focused, content focused, and content only. The new speaker focused layout prioritizes presenter video alongside shared content for greater visibility. Available for Teams events organizers on Teams for Windows desktop and Mac desktop. Fundamentals and Security Enhanced real-time alerting rule management in Teams admin center Administrators can now duplicate an existing alerting rule to create a similar configuration without rebuilding it, bulk upload users when creating or editing a rule, and delete rules directly from the management experience. These capabilities are available for in-progress meetings and calls rule types, and organizations can configure monitoring for up to 500 users across their real-time alerting rules. Security Detection Report in Teams admin center A new Security Detection Report in the Teams admin center gives admins a unified view of messaging security detections across signals such as impersonation, malicious URLs, and weaponizable file types. Admins can review detection activity in one place and export detailed data for further investigation, improving visibility into threats in Teams. Single pane for monitoring and troubleshooting meetings and calls ( Windows ) Administrators can monitor meeting and call health across the organization from one place, identifying recurring issues, uncovering trends, and proactively troubleshooting problems affecting people in both live and past meetings and calls. Meeting participant detail audit records in all participating tenants Admins can now access participant-level audit records for their own users in cross-tenant meetings, helping investigate incidents even when another organization hosted the meeting. Teams audit logging now shares meeting participant detail records with all participating tenants, not just the organizer tenant, and each record includes organizer information so admins can tell whether a meeting was organized inside or outside their tenant. Teams optimization for VDI now supports Teams Events (Windows) Attendees joining Teams Events from virtualized Windows desktops can offload audio and video to their local device, supporting high definition playback while easing load on the virtual desktop. Optimization works on Windows endpoints connecting to Azure Virtual Desktop, Windows 365, Citrix, Omnissa, or Amazon. Captions, DVR, reactions, streaming chat, and Q&A are all supported, as are first-party and third-party eCDNs. Teams Platform Real-time buying signals, now in Teams Sales Navigator for Microsoft Teams delivers real-time lead and account insights directly within Microsoft Teams.
